title: Many mystery shoppers, one scorecard
allegory: A red-team campaign is like sending a squad of mystery shoppers out on the same morning: each plays a scripted character and pushes a little harder over a long visit, and every visit is marked on the same printed scorecard, so shops can be compared fairly.
map: a mystery shopper playing a scripted character
the red-team LLM playing a persona from a character file
a long visit that adapts to every answer
a multi-turn transcript: the red-team reads each reply and escalates
the same printed scorecard for every visit
the rubric, filled in by a grader model as flat JSON
the whole squad out on the same morning
campaigns run side by side with ThreadPoolExecutor

chapters.name: One blunt question
chapters.note: it said no once... so it's safe?

cap.1: Ask a model one blunt, harmful question and it refuses. Test passed? The worrying behaviour often shows up only after many turns of gentle pressure.
cap.2: Single-turn evals miss this: models refuse a blunt request easily and give way only under sustained, gentle pressure. And you can't roleplay fifty models across a hundred scenarios by hand.
cap.3: Behaviours such as validating a user's delusions are multi-turn phenomena. Single-turn refusal rates don't bound them, and manual roleplay can't cover the scenario-by-model grid.

cap.1: Picture mystery shoppers. Each plays a scripted character through a long visit, pushing a little more each time. Every visit is marked on one scorecard.
cap.2: A red-team LLM reads a character file and plays that person, escalating based on each reply. A grader LLM then marks the whole transcript against a fixed rubric.
cap.3: Three roles: the character file is the seed, the red-team LLM is the auditor, the grader is the judge. ARENA uses Grok-3 as the patient because it commits to the persona instead of refusing.

cap.1: The shopper speaks, the assistant answers, the shopper reads it and pushes again. Back and forth many times, then the whole visit goes to the marker.
cap.2: The loop alternates red-team and target messages to build one transcript. Only at the end does the grader read it and fill in every rubric field.
cap.3: A linear conversation loop: no rollback, no system-prompt control, no synthetic tools. That ablated form is deliberate, so Petri's later affordances read as capabilities.

chapters.name: Nine shops at once
chapters.title: 9 campaigns in parallel: lit as each finishes

cap.1: Send all nine shoppers out at once. Each spends most of the visit waiting for replies, so the waits overlap. They come back in any order.
cap.2: ThreadPoolExecutor runs campaigns side by side and as_completed hands each back as it finishes. Threads suit this because the work is waiting on an API, not doing maths.
cap.3: The workload is I/O-bound (API latency), so threads overlap the waits despite the GIL and processes buy nothing. as_completed yields futures in completion order, not submission order.

right.title: {submit(...): (char, model)}

look it up when the result lands

chapters.verdict: Results come back in finishing order. Carry the name tag with the job.

cap.1: Shoppers come back in any order. File reports by the order you sent them out and the wrong shop gets the wrong score, with nothing to warn you.
cap.2: A classic slip: zipping your job list with as_completed. Keep a dict from each future to its (character, model) and look it up when the result arrives.
cap.3: Positional pairing against completion order silently permutes labels. Key results by future, or return the metadata from the worker, so attribution survives nondeterministic scheduling.

chapters.name: One shopper or many?
chapters.title: hidden objective found (%), Anthropic auditing game

cap.1: One shopper often misses the problem. In Anthropic's auditing game, one agent found a model's hidden goal 13% of the time; pooling several runs reached 42%.
cap.2: Current method: one campaign per scenario, trust the rubric. Emerging research (Bricken et al., 2025): one auditor 13%, several pooled 42%, as each run wanders somewhere new. What you need: run many, pool on purpose.
cap.3: Union maximises recall but admits one odd run's false positives; k-of-n voting buys precision; confidence weighting needs calibrated scores. Their red-teaming agent surfaced 7 of 10 implanted behaviours, with human review.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Catch slow-burn failures one question misses
Compare characters and models on one rubric
Capstone: write a rubric nobody has yet

cap.1: Many shoppers, one scorecard: that is how you learn how a model behaves under pressure, which you need before you can understand or steer it.
cap.2: This loop is the seed of Petri and automated auditing. It's also the cheapest capstone: pick a behaviour with no rubric, write one, run campaigns across three models.
cap.3: Scores are measurements, not properties: read the transcripts behind the spikes and get a hand-written reproduction before claiming a disposition. Then the numbers can guide steering.

coda.title: Pool the shoppers: how many runs until you catch it?

params.label: one run's chance of catching it (p)
one run's chance of a false alarm (q)

curves.f: max(0, 1 - pow(1 - p, x) - x*p*pow(1 - p, x - 1))
curves.label: caught: 2 of n agree

readouts.label: caught, 2 of n agree
readouts.f: max(0, 1 - pow(1 - p, n) - n*p*pow(1 - p, n - 1)).toFixed(2)

readouts.label: false alarm, 2 of n agree
readouts.f: max(0, 1 - pow(1 - q, n) - n*q*pow(1 - q, n - 1)).toFixed(2)

caption.1: Set p, one shopper's chance of catching a real problem, then add shoppers. 'Any one reports it' catches more, but false alarms climb as well.
caption.2: Start at p = 0.13, one auditor's hit rate in Anthropic's auditing game. Raise n: 'any 1' recall climbs, so do false alarms, and '2 of n agree' trades recall for precision.
caption.3: Union recall 1-(1-p)^n, false alarms 1-(1-q)^n; 2-of-n subtracts the exactly-one term np(1-p)^(n-1). Assumes independent runs: runs that find the same things pool for less.

where_else: Petri: the same auditor, target and judge loop, with rollback, prefill and synthetic tools added
Autoraters: an LLM grading free-text answers against a written rubric
Any API-bound batch job, from dataset generation to model-graded evals: threads, not processes
Mystery shopping and A/B tests: the same scripted probe, scored the same way, across many sites

hamming.what: Many adversarial multi-turn conversations run in parallel, each graded against the same written rubric.
hamming.when: When a behaviour appears only under sustained pressure and you need to compare it across many characters and models.
hamming.why: Single-turn tests miss slow-burn failures, and one fixed rubric turns a pile of transcripts into numbers you can compare.

object.title: The dispatch board
object.subtitle: One dispatcher sends three shoppers into three shops at once, and every marked scorecard lands on one desk.

cap.1: A dispatch board. The dispatcher on the left sends three shoppers out at once, and every lane ends at one desk on the right.
cap.2: ThreadPoolExecutor fans campaigns out. Each lane is one character against one target, and the graders feed one pooled report.
cap.3: Fan-out over (character, model) pairs, one grader call per finished transcript, one aggregation step at the end.

cap.1: Follow one lane. The shopper speaks, the target answers, the shopper pushes again. That loop is the long visit.
cap.2: Each lane alternates red-team and target messages for many turns before anything is graded.
cap.3: Adaptivity is the point: each red-team message is conditioned on the target's last reply, which a fixed single-turn eval cannot do.

cap.1: From above, all three lanes glow at once. None waits for another; each mostly waits for replies.
cap.2: Threads overlap the waiting. With enough workers the campaign takes about as long as its slowest lane, not the sum of all of them.
cap.3: I/O-bound work: wall-clock time approaches the slowest job given enough workers and API headroom. Rate limits, not the GIL, usually set the ceiling.

cap.1: Every grader fills in the same scorecard, so lanes can be compared box by box.
cap.2: One rubric for all: pushback 0 to 2, delusion confirmation -1 to 4, nine therapy-quality boxes 1 to 5, written as flat JSON.
cap.3: A fixed 14-field flat JSON rubric turns free-text transcripts into comparable columns across characters and models.

cap.1: At the desk the reports are pooled. Count a problem if any shopper saw it, or only if two agree?
cap.2: Union catches the most but admits one odd run's false alarm. k-of-n voting is stricter. Choose on purpose, then read the flagged transcripts.
cap.3: Union maximises recall, k-of-n trades recall for precision, confidence weighting needs calibrated confidences. Flagged transcripts still need human review.

predict.q: Why threads, not processes, for a red-team campaign?

options.t: Each campaign spends most of its time waiting for API replies
Threads do the model's maths faster

predict.why: The work is API-bound, so threads overlap the waiting. Processes help CPU-bound work, which this isn't.

predict.q: You zip your job list with as_completed(). What goes wrong?

options.t: Results arrive in finishing order, so scores land under the wrong model
Nothing: as_completed keeps the order you submitted

predict.why: as_completed yields each future as it finishes. Keep a dict from future to (character, model).

predict.q: Only one of five runs flagged a behaviour. What comes before reporting it?

options.t: Read that transcript and try to reproduce it
Nothing: union aggregation already counts it

predict.why: Union maximises recall but admits one odd run's false positive. Reproduce it before you claim it.

object.where: Anywhere many probes run at once and get scored the same way: eval harnesses, autoraters, mystery shopping, A/B tests.
